title: People Who Rush Through Tasks and Assignments
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece diagnoses why some capable team members consistently rush their work and produces a practical fix rather than a lecture on carefulness. The author traces rushing to several root causes — task overload, impatience, overconfidence, and poor planning — and argues the remedy is structural, not motivational: break work into smaller segments with mandatory checkpoints. A notable twist is the recommendation to bring peers into the review process, since social visibility often changes behavior faster than a boss's feedback. The piece closes by reminding leaders that their own deadline-setting and workload assignment can be the actual cause of the rushing they're trying to fix.
points: Rushing usually traces back to anxiety about workload, impatience and competitiveness, overconfidence, or deadline pressure rather than a simple character flaw.
Breaking work into smaller chunks with mandatory quality checkpoints forces rushers to slow down without a direct confrontation about pace.
Peer evaluation is often more effective than leader review at curbing rushed work, because people care more about how peers perceive their output.
Leaders should audit their own role first, since unrealistic deadlines and overloaded task lists can manufacture the very rushing behavior they're trying to correct.
quotes: Despite being highly skilled, their work is full of errors, and the quality of their output is lower than it should be.
For other team members, the combination of impatience and competitiveness produces a toxic elixir, driving the rush to finish work.
By establishing checkpoints, which might include interim feedback, leaders moderate team members who are too fast for their own good.
Peer evaluation tends to be even more candid, and impatient team members will often decelerate their pace, become more careful, and improve quality to ensure they are seen favorably by peers.
Quality never profits from rushing. Too much speed in anything is a recipe for missing things. Mistakes are inevitable, but rushing is always a choice.
